- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 10–30% for high sentiment periods.
- When sentiment is strongly negative (≤ -0.67), model underestimates; increase forecast by 10–30% to compensate for bearish bias.
- After a sharp price spike (forecast > 3x recent mean), model often overcorrects; apply a “lag correction” — reduce forecast by 20–50% for 3–5 days post-spike.
- If sentiment shifts from negative to positive within 3–5 days, model often fails to adjust quickly; apply a “sentiment pivot” rule — increase forecast by 15–25% if sentiment turns positive after 3 days of negativity.
- Model consistently underestimates in low-volatility periods (sentiment flat or near 0); add 5–15% to forecast if sentiment is neutral or low.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates early in the forecast window (first 5–7 days); apply a “decay filter” — reduce forecast by 10–20% for first 5 days if sentiment is neutral or mixed.
- If true outcome shows mean reversion (price drops after peak), model often fails to anticipate; apply “mean reversion buffer” — reduce forecast by 15–30% if price > 2x recent average and sentiment is neutral or negative.
